stimulus.text: Paraphrase: In November and December 1943, President Franklin Roosevelt, Prime Minister Winston Churchill, and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met for the first time together at Tehran, Iran. Stalin had long demanded that the United States and Britain open a second front in Western Europe to ease the pressure on Soviet armies, which were carrying most of the fighting against Germany. At Tehran the three leaders agreed that the Allied invasion of France would go forward in 1944, timed with a major Soviet offensive in the east. Stalin also promised that the Soviet Union would join the war against Japan once Germany was defeated. The three leaders agreed in principle to form a new international organization to keep the peace after the war.
stimulus.source_note: Original secondary summary drawn from Barron's Chapter 9 (Tehran Conference, November 1943) and Princeton Chapter 11 (first meeting of the 'big three' at Tehran).

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded paraphrases, tables, and photographs (see source_note)
stem: At Tehran, what did the three Allied leaders agree would happen in 1944?

options.text: The Soviet Union would invade Japan right away
options.misconception: Japan came later; the pledge was to join the war against Japan after Germany was defeated.

options.text: Britain would make a separate peace with Germany
options.misconception: Britain stayed in the alliance and fought in France in 1944.

options.text: The Allies would open a second front in France
The United States would leave the war in Europe
options.misconception: The United States stayed in Europe and led the invasion of France.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Stalin promised to join the war against Japan only after Germany was defeated, not at once.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Britain stayed in the alliance and fought in France in 1944.
rationales.C: The Tehran agreement timed the invasion of France with a Soviet offensive in the east, so Germany would have to fight on two fronts at once.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the United States stayed in Europe and led the invasion of France.
rationales.general:
1. The stimulus says Stalin had long demanded a second front in Western Europe.
2. At Tehran the leaders agreed the invasion of France would go forward in 1944.
3. Background: the invasion, called D-Day, landed in Normandy on June 6, 1944.
4. It was timed with a Soviet offensive, so Germany had to fight in the east and the west at once.
Remember: a second front means opening a new place to fight, which splits the enemy's strength.
